Question: What are the legal consequences of impersonating the police?
Answer: RCW 9A.60.040 Criminal impersonation in the first degree. (1) A person is guilty of criminal impersonation in the first degree if the person: (a) Assumes a false identity and does an act in his or her assumed character with intent to defraud another or for any other unlawful purpose; or (b) Pretends to be a representative of some person or organization or a public servant and does an act in his or her pretended capacity with intent to defraud another or for any other unlawful purpose. (2) Criminal impersonation in the first degree is a class C felony. Criminal impersonation in the second degree. (1) A person is guilty of criminal impersonation in the second degree if the person: (a)(i) Claims to be a law enforcement officer or creates an impression that he or she is a law enforcement officer; and (ii) Under circumstances not amounting to criminal impersonation in the first degree, does an act with intent to convey the impression that he or she is acting in an official capacity and a reasonable person would believe the person is a law enforcement officer; or (b) Falsely assumes the identity of a veteran or active duty member of the armed forces of the United States with intent to defraud for the purpose of personal gain or to facilitate any unlawful activity. (2) Criminal impersonation in the second degree is a gross misdemeanor.

Question: Is it legal for police to run your name through the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) without a valid reason?
Answer: I guess that depends on what you consider to be a “valid reason.” I taught myself to run the various queries and reports available through NCIC by running the names of people I knew for warrants, driver license status, criminal history, vehicle registration, etc. (big surprise when your mom pops up as a fugitive felon) at our new CRT-equipped terminal, as opposed to the teletype we had for years. This was then, as now, illegal as hell, as I had not the smallest thread of a genuine criminal justice purpose in so doing. However, I’m pretty sure the statutes of limitations has run, 40 years later. There are now greater safeguards on inquiries, although curious cops and dispatchers can still sneak in the occasional recreational inquiry. If they get caught doing it, the FBI has a reputation for going after these crimes with vigor, as a way of making an example to others thinking about such a caper. So, no, it is not “legal” (the proper term in “lawful”) to run your name through NCIC without a valid reason. The distinction is that you may not consider their reason to be valid, while it was lawful under the circumstances.

Question: Is it true that you need to do a court order before you can get your fingerprints and photo removed from the database?
Answer: Probably, and you might not be successful. Most criminal justice systems maintain or use multiple information databases. There might be one for Anytown PD, another for all the agencies in the bi- or tri-county Anytown area, a state-level database, and the Big Kahuna, the National Criminal Information Center, aka NCIC. NCIC is owned and operated by the FBI. If you have been fingerprinted by a law enforcement agency, your prints and associated data are in all of those systems. You often have to petition each one to delete your records, and give them a good reason why they should do it. Say you get a court order to expunge your records from the kindly old Justice of the Peace in Anytown. The Anytown PD will probably comply. Don’t count on that being a total erasure. There will still be cops who remember the case, and there may be some reports that reference it. It’s all but impossible to chase this stuff down 100%. The regional and state databases might go along, but it’s an even bet they’ll tell you to get your order from a higher court. You’ll have to convince a judge in the court of general jurisdiction that it is in the public interest to purge your prints. That might be a tough sell. Where you’re really going to get pushback is from the FBI. They’ll tell you the state court has no jurisdiction over a federal agency (and they will be correct). You can try and get an order from a federal court, but don’t be surprised if you are shot down. How does having those prints in the system affect you? Unless you continue on a life of crime, there will likely be zero impact. My prints and mug shot have been in the system since 1968, when I had a summer job with the city where I grew up (good luck trying to recognize me today from that mug shot). I have since been printed many times, as I have been a public employee most of my life and those jobs required being fingerprinted. The only time it had any effect at all was a few years ago when I applied for a Known Traveler Number with the TSA. The KTN allows me to use the TSA PreCheck line at the airport and get through security faster. I was told the KTN would come through a little faster if my prints were already in the system. I had the KTN two days later. On the other end of the spectrum, say that you get printed for whatever minor crime you did, and the prints remain in the system. Twenty years from now, your latent print is developed off of a flash drive or whatever data storage device people will be using then, and the flash drive contains child pornography. The police will be looking to have an up close and personal chat with you. I suggest you bring a lawyer.

Question: Can people with implants be legally diagnosed as disabled and take up all my famous parking spots?
Answer: I’m not sure why you regard handicapped spaces as your “famous parking spots,” but, otherwise, yes. “Implants” can be hip or knee replacements. Some people gain restored mobility after these implants are installed, but others still experience pain or limited tolerance to walking. If their physician feels they are sufficiently impaired to merit a handicapped parking placard, they can give them the documentation needed to obtain one. The disability of the person holding the placard may not be immediately apparent. My former girlfriend had a degenerative neurological disorder. Sometimes she would be able to walk with no perceptible problem, but when she became fatigued, it would invite what she called a “storm” and her gait would be severely impaired, so much that I occasionally had to go fetch her wheelchair from the car and bring it to her to get back. We got a few dirty looks when we got out of the car at some retail establishments where she didn’t think she would have to walk very far, or when she could use a shopping cart as a support while we went through the store. The moral of the story: don’t judge the person getting out of the car just because they don't have an obvious impairment.

Question: Does it take a lot more intelligence to be a detective than the police?
Answer: First, detectives are the police. A detective is just a uniformed police officer who has an assignment other than uniformed patrol. TV detectives tend to act like exalted royalty among “uniforms,” but at most places the relationship is far more congenial. I regularly worked with detectives who had been my trainees when they were rookies. One got kind of full of himself. He was well-connected in the department and got an assignment to narcotics shortly after completing probation. One night, I and another patrol officer were assigned to assist the narcs with serving several search warrants. We went in first, so anyone inside would know it was the real police and not pretenders. We had parked our patrol cars and ridden to the search warrant venues in the narcs’ unmarked van. When we were all done, my former rookie asked his supervisor, “Sarge, you want me to take the uniforms back to their cars?” I interrupted the conversation to say, “Officer ______, did you just refer to your former field training officer as a ‘uniform?”” There was an uncomfortable pause before he answered, “Yes, sir. Sorry, sir.” He called me “sir” for about a year afterward. I worked with some detectives who were unquestionably smart people, and others who had to concentrate to remember how to grunt. The same was true of uniformed patrol officers, as that was where everyone started. Assignments to detectives had a lot more to do with one political connections and standing than with IQ points. In fact, my agency had three card-carrying members of Mensa while I worked there. We were all uniformed patrol officers. Many questions I get on Quora come from people who believe they can be hired into law enforcement and immediately start work as a detective. Doesn’t happen. You may luck out or be well-connected and get an early detective assignment, but it’s more likely you’ll work in uniformed patrol, chasing the radio and taking reports, for five to ten years before you get a shot at detectives. And, whether you do or not doesn’t have a lot to do with your IQ.

Question: How can those who oppose execution justly say it costs more to execute a criminal than to keep them in prison for all of their life when all the extra costs, hearings, evaluations and appeals are contrived, being denied of those who are up for life?
Answer: You answered your own question. In a death penalty appeal, the state is usually funding both sides of the proceeding. The condemned prisoner has one or more attorneys doing research, filing briefs, and arguing appeals on the prisoner’s behalf, while the prosecutor’s office is answering the same arguments. These appeals go on for many years, and the meter is running the entire time. Meanwhile, the condemned prisoner has to be held in single-cell custody on the prison’s death row. This special housing can cost 2X or more to facilitate. The cost of housing prisoners varies considerably. There is a breakdown of death penalty costs here. It costs around $35,000 per year to house a regular inmate in prison. If the inmate is sentenced to life and lives for 50 years, that’s $1.75 million, although the cost will almost certainly increase with time. Compare that to the cost of a death penalty case, around $5,000,000, indictment to execution.
